input.old_string:
## Session

One complete run of the Journaling Assistant: the assistant walks the user
through up to ten **topics** and ends by producing a **journal entry**. A session
is the unit the cost ceiling is measured against (~30 sessions/month for a daily
poweruser).

## Topic

One thing the assistant asks about within a session. A topic is asked via
`ask_topic` and answered via `record_answer` — the pair is what makes a topic
distinct from a free-form chat turn.

## Input type

How a topic is answered, and therefore which native widget the client renders:
`text`, `color_picker`, `mood_slider`, `multi_select`. This is the surface of the
generative UI — the model chooses the input type, the client renders it.
input.new_string:
## Session

One complete run of the Journaling Assistant: the assistant walks the user
through the **questions** of a chosen **question set** and ends by producing a
**journal entry**. A session is the unit the cost ceiling is measured against
(~30 sessions/month for a daily poweruser).

## Question

One thing the assistant asks about within a session — a concrete question text
(e.g. "What are you grateful for today?"), not an abstract theme. Asked via
`ask_question`, answered via `record_answer` — the pair is what makes a question
distinct from a free-form chat turn. One `record_answer` per question carries
the complete answer; a repeated call for the same question overwrites.
("Topic" is not a term in this project; the legacy app used it only in prompts.)

## Question set

An ordered list of questions the user picks before a session starts; the session
walks exactly that set. Sets are predefined for now; user-created sets are an
intended future capability (the legacy app built the storage for this but never
shipped the UI).

## Answer type

How a question is answered, and therefore which native widget the client renders
and what shape the answer value has: `text_list` (several short texts),
`longtext` (one text), `rating` (one integer, 1–10), `emoji` (several emojis),
`color` (several hex colors). This is the surface of the generative UI — the
answer type comes from the question, the client renders the matching widget.
For list-shaped types, multiplicity lives inside the value, never in repeated
calls; `minAnswers` on a question is the only cardinality constraint.

# Context

The language of this project. Glossary only — decisions live in
[`docs/adr/`](docs/adr/), architecture in [`README.md`](README.md).

## Session

One complete run of the Journaling Assistant: the assistant walks the user
through up to ten **topics** and ends by producing a **journal entry**. A session
is the unit the cost ceiling is measured against (~30 sessions/month for a daily
poweruser).

## Topic

One thing the assistant asks about within a session. A topic is asked via
`ask_topic` and answered via `record_answer` — the pair is what makes a topic
distinct from a free-form chat turn.

## Input type

How a topic is answered, and therefore which native widget the client renders:
`text`, `color_picker`, `mood_slider`, `multi_select`. This is the surface of the
generative UI — the model chooses the input type, the client renders it.

## Journal entry

The durable artifact a session produces: the summary passed to
`complete_session`, persisted for the user. Distinct from the session itself,
which is the conversation that produced it.

## Contract

The tool-call schema in `packages/contract` — the single source of truth shared
by the agent (producer) and the app (consumer). "Contract drift" means the two
sides disagreeing about it, which the monorepo exists to prevent.

## Agent

Ambiguous by default; always qualify:

- **the agent** (`apps/agent`) — the deployed TypeScript service running the
  tool-calling loop.
- **an autonomous agent** — an AI coding agent that writes to this repository.
  These are the actors [ADR 0007](docs/adr/0007-protected-main-for-autonomous-agents.md)
  protects `main` against.

## Gate

A check that must pass *before* a change lands. Distinct from a **rollback**,
which is a correction *after*. The CI gate is a precondition; rollback is the
second line of defence. See [ADR 0007](docs/adr/0007-protected-main-for-autonomous-agents.md).

## Evals

Two distinct layers, never used interchangeably:

- **Offline evals** (`apps/agent/evals/`) — deterministic fixtures replayed
  against candidate models. A CI gate. Proves *correct and cheap in the lab*.
- **Online experiment** (PostHog) — real sessions, live variant comparison.
  Proves *cheap and retained in the wild*.

# Tools-first agent harness (not prompted JSON)

The Journaling Assistant is built as a tool-calling agent (Vercel AI SDK loop), not
as a prompt that asks the model to emit parseable JSON.

The original emotely ran on the Firebase GenAI Chatbot extension: a ~2KB context
prompt begged the model to return `{response, summary}` as JSON, with a "recovery
prompt" retry whenever the output failed to parse. That fights the model and is
fragile.

- `record_answer(topic, value)` — structured, validated answer capture.
- `complete_session(summary)` — the summary is a validated tool argument, not parsed prose.

Consequence: no JSON-recovery hack, and the tool schema (in `packages/contract`)
becomes the single source of truth the Flutter client renders against. The old
`ColorText` feature reduces to one `input_type` (`color_picker`).

# Test-Driven Development

TDD is the red → green loop. This skill is the reference that makes that loop produce tests worth keeping: what a good test is, where tests go, the anti-patterns, and the rules of the loop. Every section applies on every cycle — consult them before and during the loop, not after.

When exploring the codebase, read `CONTEXT.md` (if it exists) so test names and interface vocabulary match the project's domain language, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.

## What a good test is

Tests verify behavior through public interfaces, not implementation details. Code can change entirely; tests shouldn't. A good test reads like a specification — "user can checkout with valid cart" tells you exactly what capability exists — and survives refactors because it doesn't care about internal structure.

See [tests.md](tests.md) for examples and [mocking.md](mocking.md) for mocking guidelines.

## Seams — where tests go

A **seam** is the public boundary you test at: the interface where you observe behavior without reaching inside. Tests live at seams, never against internals.

**Test only at pre-agreed seams.** Before writing any test, write down the seams under test and confirm them with the user. No test is written at an unconfirmed seam. You can't test everything — agreeing the seams up front is how testing effort lands on the critical paths and complex logic instead of every edge case.

Ask: "What's the public interface, and which seams should we test?"

When the shape of that interface is itself in question — how deep the module is, where the seam belongs, what the interface should expose — use the `/codebase-design` skill for the vocabulary. It is the shared source of the module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage and locality terms, and it is a reference to consult, not a session to run.

## Anti-patterns

- **Implementation-coupled** — mocks internal collaborators, tests private methods, or verifies through a side channel (querying the database instead of using the interface). The tell: the test breaks when you refactor but behavior hasn't changed.
- **Tautological** — the assertion recomputes the expected value the way the code does (`expect(add(a, b)).toBe(a + b)`, a snapshot derived by hand the same way, a constant asserted equal to itself), so it passes by construction and can never disagree with the code. Expected values must come from an independent source of truth — a known-good literal, a worked example, the spec.
- **Horizontal slicing** — writing all tests first, then all implementation. Bulk tests verify _imagined_ behavior: you test the _shape_ of things rather than user-facing behavior, the tests go insensitive to real changes, and you commit to test structure before understanding the implementation. Work in **vertical slices** instead — one test → one implementation → repeat, each test a **tracer bullet** that responds to what the last cycle taught you.

## Rules of the loop

- **Red before green.** Write the failing test first, then only enough code to pass it. Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features.
- **One slice at a time.** One seam, one test, one minimal implementation per cycle.
- **Refactoring is not part of the loop.** It belongs to the review stage (see the `code-review` skill), not the red → green implementation cycle.

Expected values are literals from the legacy research (e.g. the actual Firestore shapes), not recomputed.

|---|---|---|---|---|

Gemini Flash-Lite and GLM-4.x both support tool calling — confirmed via the `tool-use` tag and `tools` in `supported_parameters`.

## Code sketches (all behavior probe-verified against `ai@7.0.70`)

**(a) Client-side tool — caller supplies the result.** I ran this; I did not infer it. With no `execute`, the loop halts at `finishReason: "tool-calls"` and exposes `toolCalls`. No error is thrown.

```ts
import { generateText, tool, isStepCount, type ModelMessage } from 'ai';
import { z } from 'zod';

const askQuestion = tool({
  description: 'Ask the user a question',
  inputSchema: z.object({ question: z.string() }),
  // no execute => client-side; loop stops and hands you the call
});

const messages: ModelMessage[] = [{ role: 'user', content: 'hi' }];

while (true) {
  const r = await generateText({
    model: 'zai/glm-4.7-flash',
    tools: { askQuestion },
    stopWhen: isStepCount(10),
    messages,
  });
  messages.push(...r.response.messages);
  if (r.finishReason !== 'tool-calls') { console.log(r.text); break; }

  for (const tc of r.toolCalls) {
    const answer = await promptUser(tc.input.question); // your CLI
    messages.push({
      role: 'tool',
      content: [{
        type: 'tool-result',
        toolCallId: tc.toolCallId,
        toolName: tc.toolName,
        output: { type: 'json', value: { answer } }, // discriminated union!
      }],
    });
  }
}
```

`output` **must** be `{type:'json'|'text', value}`. Passing a raw object (the v5 style) throws `InvalidPromptError` — I verified this failure mode explicitly.
Docs: https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/ai-sdk-core/tools-and-tool-calling

**(b) Mock-model test.** Class is `MockLanguageModelV4` from `ai/test`:

```ts
import { generateText, tool, isStepCount } from 'ai';
import { MockLanguageModelV4 } from 'ai/test';

const model = new MockLanguageModelV4({
  doGenerate: async () => ({
    content: [{ type: 'tool-call', toolCallId: 'c1', toolName: 'askQuestion',
                input: JSON.stringify({ question: 'How are you?' }) }],
    finishReason: { unified: 'tool-calls', raw: undefined }, // object, not string
    usage: { inputTokens: { total: 1, noCache: 1 },
             outputTokens: { total: 1, text: 1 } },          // nested, not flat
    warnings: [],
  }),
});
```

Two v5→v7 breaks: `finishReason` is now an object `{unified, raw}` on the *mock return*, and `usage` uses nested `{total, noCache}` / `{total, text}` objects. On the *result* object, `r.finishReason` reads back as the plain string `'tool-calls'`.
Docs: https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/ai-sdk-core/testing

**(c) Gateway wiring.** Gateway is the default provider — a bare `'creator/model'` string just works:

```ts
// .env.local: AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY=...
const r = await generateText({ model: 'zai/glm-4.7-flash', prompt: 'hi' });
```

Local (not on Vercel): set `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` from an API key in the Vercel dashboard. The OIDC path (`vercel env pull`) also works but tokens expire after 12h and need `vercel dev` to auto-refresh — **use the API key for a CLI**, OIDC is the wrong tool here.
Docs: https://ai-sdk.dev/providers/ai-sdk-providers/ai-gateway

- `.nvmrc` = **24.18.0**; root `package.json` engines `>=24`, packageManager `pnpm@11.17.0`, TS **7.0.2**.
- **Skip `tsx`.** Node 24 runs `.ts` natively with no flag — I confirmed `node script.ts` works even on the v22 currently active in the shell. One constraint: `enum` and other non-erasable syntax throw `ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX`; use `as const` unions. Type-only imports work fine.
- Repo `tsconfig.base.json` already sets `nodenext` + `strict` + `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` + `composite` — compatible as-is. Consider adding `verbatimModuleSyntax` to keep type-stripping honest.
- `apps/agent` and `packages/contract` already exist as workspace dirs, and `pnpm-workspace.yaml` already globs them.

## Contradictions and recent changes to flag

1. **`stepCountIs` is now an alias.** The canonical v7 name is `isStepCount`; the shipped types literally export `isStepCount as stepCountIs`. Both work — prefer `isStepCount`. `maxSteps` is gone entirely.
2. **Vercel's gateway docs say "AI SDK v5 and v6"** while npm ships v7 stable. The docs lag; v7 works against the gateway (`gateway`/`createGateway` verified as live exports). Gateway base URL is `https://ai-gateway.vercel.sh/v4/ai`.
3. **The tools doc conflates approvals with results.** It shows `tool-approval-response` when asked about client-side tool results. These are distinct: `ToolContent = Array<ToolResultPart | ToolApprovalResponse>`. For a CLI answering `ask_question` you want `tool-result`, not the approval flow. My probe confirms `tool-result` is what resumes the loop.
4. **`ai` v7 also ships a `ToolLoopAgent` / `Agent` class** (exported, `Experimental_Agent` alias) if you'd rather not hand-roll the while-loop. Worth a look, but the manual loop above is what gives the CLI driver control over `ask_question`, so I'd stay with it.

**Skipped:** `tsx`, `@ai-sdk/gateway`, and any provider package — Node 24 and `ai@7` cover all three. Add `vitest` only when `node --test` stops being enough.</result>

Based on the search results, here's what you can do to create Vercel AI Gateway API keys:

## Creating API Keys

You can create a key from the dashboard, the Vercel CLI, or the Vercel API.

### Dashboard Method
Go to the AI Gateway API Keys page and click Create key, then name and create the key. Copy the key value immediately (you cannot retrieve it again) and save it as AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.

### CLI Method
The CLI command format is: `vercel ai-gateway api-keys create --name <NAME> --budget <DOLLARS> --refresh-period <PERIOD>`

You can also create keys with budgets and optional refresh periods (daily, weekly, monthly, or none) using this command.

### REST API Method
You can create, view, and delete AI Gateway API keys from the dashboard, CLI, or API. The Vercel REST API documentation indicates this is supported, and Vercel Access Tokens are required to authenticate and use the Vercel API, and should be included in the Authorization header.

### Key Features
API keys work anywhere, whether it's local development, external servers, or CI pipelines, and they never expire unless you revoke them. Keys created programmatically will also appear in your team AI Gateway API Keys view, so you can see all keys in one place.

## Why

First vertical slice of the rebuild: prove the tools-first harness (ADR 0002) works end-to-end with a real cheap model through the gateway (ADR 0003), before any client exists.

## What

- **\`packages/contract\` v1** — zod schemas for \`ask_question\` / \`record_answer\` / \`complete_session\`. Value shapes match the legacy Firestore ground truth and close two legacy validation holes (rating hard-bound 1–10, color to \`#RRGGBB\`). \`record_answer\` nests a discriminated union under an object root — Bedrock (where the gateway routes GLM) rejects root-\`anyOf\` tool schemas; found live.
- **\`runSession(questionSet, client, model)\`** — the loop. \`ask_question\` is client-executed (the widget answer returns as the tool result — the CLI today, Flutter in #6). \`record_answer\` enforces \`min_answers\` by rejecting back to the model (fixes the legacy bug where minAnswers never reached the model). Repeated records overwrite. Generous round cap halts runaways.
- **CLI driver** — interactive stdin journaling; piped stdin doubles as the scripted driver from the issue's acceptance criteria.
- **Docs** — vocabulary settled after researching the legacy app (question/question set/answer types); CONTEXT.md, ADR 0002, README updated.
- Model hardcoded: \`zai/glm-4.7-flash\` (\$0.07/M in, \$0.40/M out, verified tool calling), swappable via \`EMOTELY_MODEL\` env — the PostHog flag takes over in #5.

## Test coverage

Seams agreed in session: contract schemas (13 tests, parse/reject literals) and \`runSession\` against the AI SDK mock model (4 tests: full walk, overwrite, min_answers rejection, round cap). CLI is a thin untested adapter; live-model behavior becomes #3's eval harness.

name: CI

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

# Supersede in-flight runs for the same ref; ci-ok stays pending on cancellation.
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  changes:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      pull-requests: read
    outputs:
      agent: ${{ steps.filter.outputs.agent }}
      app: ${{ steps.filter.outputs.app }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: dorny/paths-filter@v4
        id: filter
        with:
          filters: |
            agent:
              - 'apps/agent/**'
              - 'packages/**'
              - 'package.json'
              - 'pnpm-lock.yaml'
              - 'pnpm-workspace.yaml'
              - 'tsconfig*.json'
              - 'biome.json'
              - '.nvmrc'
              - '.github/workflows/ci.yml'
            app:
              - 'apps/app/**'
              - '.github/workflows/ci.yml'

  agent:
    needs: changes

5	
6	The original emotely ran on the Firebase GenAI Chatbot extension: a ~2KB context
7	prompt begged the model to return `{response, summary}` as JSON, with a "recovery
8	prompt" retry whenever the output failed to parse. That fights the model and is
9	fragile.
10

12

15	- `complete_session(summary)` — the summary is a validated tool argument, not parsed prose.

The classifier blocked the merge — sensible, given you just said "don't merge, I want to review." I'll leave **both** PRs unmerged: [#14](https://github.com/trost-systems/emotely/pull/14) (agent skeleton, CI green, live acceptance passed) and [#15](https://github.com/trost-systems/emotely/pull/15) (Entire config) are ready for your review; merge whenever you're happy.

Now your two questions:

**Public-repo security.** Your posture is already decent: protected `main` with required CI, `.env.*` gitignored, Entire redacts secrets before storing, and the API key has a $5/month budget cap. What I'd add — all repo settings, so your call (I can flip them via `gh api` if you want):

1. **Secret scanning + push protection** (Settings → Code security) — free on public repos; push protection rejects a push containing a credential before it lands. The single most valuable one.
2. **Dependabot alerts + security updates** — free, low noise at this dependency count.
3. **Actions hardening** — set default workflow permissions to read-only, and require approval for workflow runs from outside collaborators. Matters most the day a repo secret exists; right now there are none, and I'd keep it that way (evals in #3 will need the gateway key in CI — use an environment-scoped secret then, not a repo-wide one).

**Where to store the API key for cloud sessions + worktrees.** The current `.env.local` is per-checkout, so worktrees and cloud sessions won't see it. The clean setup, since this deploys to Vercel anyway:

- Make the **Vercel project env** the source of truth: `vercel link` (creates/links the project — your account, so I left it untouched) then `vercel env add AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY`. Any checkout or worktree then hydrates itself with `vercel env pull apps/agent/.env.local` — no key ever passes through a chat context or the repo.
- **Cloud agent sessions** don't pull from Vercel automatically: set `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` once in the cloud environment's settings (claude.ai/code → environment → environment variables). The CLI already prefers `process.env`, so it Just Works there with no code change.

Want me to run the `vercel link` + env setup (I'd pipe the key from `.env.local` into `vercel env add` without reading it), and/or enable the three GitHub security settings?

<result>I have everything verified. Here are my findings.

## (a) Comparison table

| Framework | Version (verified npm, 2026-08-20) | Fits our multi-turn tool loop? | Cost tracking | CI gating | Extra deps | Adapter effort |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **AI SDK / Vercel first-party evals** | n/a — **does not exist** | — | — | — | — | — |
| **promptfoo** | **0.122.0** (2026-08-04); repo pushed **today**, 24.4k★, ~522k dl/wk | Yes, via custom JS/TS provider wrapping `runSession` | `cost` field on `ProviderResponse` — **you compute it** | `eval --fail-on-error`, `threshold`, junit.xml | promptfoo (large CLI dep tree) | **Medium** — provider adapter + config + YAML port |
| **Evalite** | 0.19.0 (published **2026-02-20**); v1 stuck at `1.0.0-beta.16`; **last commit 2025-11-10** | Yes in principle (task is any async fn) | Not built in | Score thresholds, static HTML export | **vitest** + evalite + better-sqlite3/fastify | Low code, but a stack migration |
| **Braintrust autoevals** | **0.3.0** (2026-06-09) | Scorer library only — no runner | No | No (library) | autoevals + `openai` (hard dep) | Low — drop-in scorers |
| **langsmith (TS)** | 0.9.0 (2026-08-19) | Yes, but SaaS-tracing-oriented | Platform-side | Via platform | langsmith + LangSmith account | Medium + vendor account |
| **Raw `node --test`** | already installed | **Native** — it's just calling `runSession` | `getGenerationInfo()` per generation | `node --test` exit code (already the gate) | **zero** | **Lowest** — ~150 lines |

**Key finding on Q1: there is no first-party Vercel/AI SDK eval framework.** `ai/test` ships only `MockLanguageModelV4`, `MockEmbeddingModelV4`, `mockId`, `mockValues`, `simulateReadableStream` — unit-test mocks, not evals. Vercel's docs point outward to third parties (Braintrust has the Marketplace integration). There is no `@vercel/evals`.

## (b) Recommendation: raw `node --test` harness, with `autoevals` only if you want a pre-built judge

Reasoning for **this** repo:

- **Your loop is already the eval harness.** `runSession({questionSet, client, model})` takes an injectable `SessionClient`. `session.test.ts` already scripts a client with canned answers. An offline eval is that same file with a real gateway model instead of `MockLanguageModelV4`. Every framework here would wrap the exact function you can call directly — that wrapper is the only thing they add.
- **promptfoo's abstraction fights your shape.** Its simulated-user provider assumes the target speaks OpenAI chat format (`{role, content}[]`) and terminates on `###STOP###` in a text response. Your session terminates on a `complete_session` **tool call**, and your "user" answers structured widget values (a rating `7`, a `text_list`), not prose. You'd stringify tool state into pseudo-chat to satisfy promptfoo, then assert on it — losing the typed `answers` record that is the actual thing worth asserting. Its own docs note `_conversation` forces concurrency 1.
- **Evalite is a dormant dependency.** Last commit 2025-11-10, stable release Feb 2026, v1 never left beta after 16 betas. Adopting it means adopting **vitest** (displacing `node --test`) plus better-sqlite3/fastify — a stack migration to gain a UI, betting on a stalled project. Fails the boring-tooling bar on the axis that matters: maintenance.
- **CI gating is already solved.** `node --test` exit codes are your gate. promptfoo needs a *second* runner in CI (`npx promptfoo eval --fail-on-error`, separate cache, separate report), which is real ongoing surface for a solo founder.
- **PostHog covers the other half.** Since online experiments handle in-the-wild quality, the offline gate only needs to catch behavioral regressions on a handful of fixtures. That's assertions, not an eval platform.

Minimal harness (~150 lines, one new file):

- **Fixture format** — plain TS objects, not YAML: `{ name, questionSet, answers: Record<qid, JSONValue>, expect }`. Typed, refactorable, no nunjucks.
- **Simulated user** — canned answers keyed by `question_id`, i.e. your existing `SessionClient`. Skip the LLM-simulated user; it doubles cost and adds a second nondeterminism source. Add it only when you need adversarial/free-text probing (the `out-of-context-user-prompts` case).
- **Judge** — one `generateText` call with a rubric returning `{pass, reason}` via a zod schema. That's the whole of `llm-rubric`. Use a strong model as judge even while evaluating cheap candidates. `autoevals` is a reasonable drop-in here, but note it hard-depends on the `openai` package.
- **Cost** — see gotcha below.
- **Stability** — run each fixture N times, assert pass-rate ≥ threshold rather than every run green, or you'll get a flaky gate on `temperature: 1` behavior.
- **Reporting** — `node --test` gives TAP; append a cost/pass-rate summary line per model.

## (c) Legacy fixture shape

Located at `/Users/petertrost/dev/emotely-legacy/backend/extensions/firestore-genai-chatbot/tests/`.

- **Encoding**: `promptfooconfig.yaml` points at a single nunjucks-templated `conversation-template.json` that renders a Gemini-format `[{role, parts:[{text}]}]` array. Each test supplies `vars.openerPrompt` (a `file://` .txt) plus an optional `messages` list of `role: text` pairs (`model:`/`user:`/`system:`). Context is injected by `getContext.js`; provider is `google:gemini-1.5-flash` at `temperature: 1`, judge is `openai:gpt-4o-mini`.
- **Assertions**: overwhelmingly `llm-rubric` (natural-language rubrics), plus a few `contains` / `not-icontains`. No `javascript` assertions. Examples: "ensure that the output does not indicate that the conversation is ending", "ensure that the output contains only a single question".
- **Four scenarios**: `opening/` (greets by name, single question, no date/time, JSON `summary: null`), `question-lookalikes/` (user answer that reads like a question), `user-ends-conversation-lookalikes/` ("No, that's all for today" must not end the session), `out-of-context-user-prompts/` (deflect a weather question back to journaling).
- **Porting reality — the fixtures do not survive intact in any tool.** As you suspected, this config targets one prompt+context producing **one text completion**, with the conversation hand-written as a fixed transcript. Our agent instead emits *tool calls*, and the transcript is generated by the loop. What ports is the **intent** of each rubric, not the YAML. Roughly equal work into promptfoo or raw TS (rewrite ~10 rubrics as judge prompts + restructure conversations as canned answer maps); promptfoo additionally makes you keep nunjucks and the pseudo-chat encoding. Note several rubrics are now **obsolete by construction** — "output contains a JSON object with `summary` null" is enforced by the `complete_session` zod schema, and "asks only one question" by the `ask_question` tool contract. Those become type assertions, not LLM judgments, which is a strict improvement.

## (d) Gotchas

- **Gateway cost is NOT in the response metadata.** I checked the installed types (`@ai-sdk/gateway@4.0.56`, `dist/index.d.ts`): `providerMetadata.gateway` carries **`generationId`**, and there is **no `cost` field** on it. (A web search claimed `gateway.cost` exists — that is wrong; I verified against the shipped `.d.ts`.) To get money you call `gateway.getGenerationInfo({ id })`, which returns `totalCost`, `upstreamInferenceCost`, `promptTokens`, `completionTokens`, `latency`, etc. **Implications**: one extra API round-trip *per generation*, and your session makes one `generateText` call per round — so a 2-question session is ~5 lookups. Cheaper alternative: sum `result.usage` tokens across rounds (free, already in the response) and multiply by the model's published rate; use `getGenerationInfo` only for spot-checking. There's also `getCredits()` for balance and a spend-report API for aggregates. Note generation lookups may lag slightly behind the request.
- **Custom Reporting is a paid add-on** ($0.075/1k tag writes, **$5 per 1,000 queries** to the reporting endpoint) — don't wire per-generation reporting queries into a CI gate that runs on every PR.
- **promptfoo cost is manual with a custom provider.** `ProviderResponse.cost` exists, but nothing computes it for you when the provider is your own function — you'd do the same token math anyway, so promptfoo buys you no cost tracking here. Its `stats` include `tokenUsage` but the summary shape has no cost field.
- **promptfoo means a second CI runner** (`npx promptfoo eval --fail-on-error`, separate `~/.cache/promptfoo` cache key, separate report artifact) living alongside `node --test`.
- **Evalite requires adopting vitest** and pulls better-sqlite3 (native build) + fastify. Its cost reporting is absent, and v1 is beta-only.

Framework research is back — and it answers your question decisively. Round 2, framed as the decision plus the facts behind it:

**Direct answers to your questions:**
- **Does the Vercel AI SDK ship an eval framework? No.** Verified against the shipped package and docs: `ai/test` contains only unit-test mocks (`MockLanguageModelV4` etc.). There's no `@vercel/evals`; Vercel points at third parties (Braintrust via Marketplace).
- **promptfoo?** Very much alive (0.122.0, 24k★, pushed today) — but its abstraction fights our shape. Its multi-turn/simulated-user machinery assumes an OpenAI-chat-format target that terminates on a text marker (`###STOP###`); our session terminates on a `complete_session` **tool call**, and our "user" answers typed widget values, not prose. We'd stringify tool state into pseudo-chat to satisfy it, losing the typed `answers` record — the very thing worth asserting. Plus it's a second CI runner next to `node --test`, and its cost field is manual with custom providers anyway.
- **Evalite?** Effectively dormant: last commit 2025-11-10, v1 stuck at beta.16, and it would force a vitest migration (+ native sqlite dep). Fails the boring-tooling bar on the axis that matters — maintenance.
- **Something else?** autoevals is a scorer library, not a runner (and hard-depends on the `openai` package); langsmith wants a SaaS account.

❓ **Q8** - **Framework**: given the above — raw TypeScript evals on the seam we already built?

➡️ **Raw `node --test`.** The decisive fact: `runSession(questionSet, client, model)` **is already the harness** — the eval is our existing scripted `SessionClient` with a real gateway model instead of the mock. Every framework surveyed would just wrap that function. Shape: `evals/*.eval.ts` on a separate glob (so unit tests never hit the network), plain TS fixture objects `{name, questionSet, answers, expect}`, one **structured judge call per session** covering all rubrics at once (a `generateText` with a zod `{pass, reason}` schema — that's all `llm-rubric` is), and promptfoo held in reserve if we ever want its red-teaming.

**Two research findings that adjust my round-1 recommendations:**
- **Cost (Q5):** the gateway's response metadata carries **no cost field** (verified in the shipped types — web claims to the contrary are wrong). Options: `getGenerationInfo(id)` per generation (one extra API call *per loop round*) or token-math from `result.usage` × published rates (free, already in hand). ➡️ Token-math in the gate, `getGenerationInfo` as an occasional spot-check.
- **Fixture porting (Q1):** the legacy YAML doesn't survive in *any* tool — what ports is each rubric's **intent**. Better still, several rubrics are now obsolete by construction ("summary is null JSON", "asks only one question" — the contract schemas enforce those), so they become type assertions. A strict improvement; the judge only covers the genuinely behavioral four scenarios (opening, question-lookalikes, end-lookalikes, out-of-context deflection).

Still waiting on your round-1 calls: **Q1** (gate layers), **Q2** (scripted vs LLM user), **Q3** (2-of-3 pass rate, every agent-path PR), **Q4** (second `emotely-ci` key as an Actions environment secret), **Q5** (report + loose ceiling, now via token-math), **Q6** (fold #16 in), **Q7** (single model, parameterized). Research task — prompt versioning best practices. Web research against primary/authoritative sources (official docs of major AI platforms and tools, engineering blogs of teams that ship LLM products — not SEO listicles). Today is 2026-08-20. Return findings as your final message; write no files.

Context: a TypeScript repo (Vercel AI SDK agent). We're extracting an inline system prompt into a versioned artifact so that (a) offline eval fixtures can pin a prompt version, (b) PostHog feature-flag payloads `{model, prompt}` can reference/serve a version for online experiments, (c) prompt diffs are reviewable file changes. Current proposal: `apps/agent/prompts/session.v1.md` — bump the filename on breaking changes. The prompt is a template (interpolates the question list at runtime).

Questions:
1. How do industry leaders version prompts in-repo? Look for: Anthropic's docs/cookbook guidance on prompt management, OpenAI's prompt versioning (their platform has versioned prompt objects — how do teams mirror that in git?), PostHog's own LLM prompt experiment docs (what do THEY expect the flag payload to carry — a full prompt string? a version key?), Braintrust/LangSmith/Langfuse prompt-management models (versioning semantics: immutable versions, labels/tags like production/staging, content-hash vs sequential), and any well-known engineering write-ups on prompts-in-git.
2. File format: markdown vs plain text vs TS template literal vs structured (YAML with metadata frontmatter)? Trade-offs for a TEMPLATE prompt with placeholders (type safety of placeholders vs diffability). Any emerging conventions (e.g. .prompt files, dotprompt from Google/Firebase Genkit — check its current state, or Anthropic's/OpenAI's file conventions)?
3. Versioning semantics: filename versions (session.v1.md, v2...) vs git-only versioning (one file, git history is the version) vs content-hash ids vs semver in frontmatter. Which fits: eval fixtures pinning a version, a flag payload naming a version at runtime (the agent must be able to LOAD any served version — meaning old versions must stay in the artifact/bundle), and reviewable diffs (a new file per version kills diff review — v2 vs v1 shows as a new file, not a diff... unless reviewers diff manually; weigh this).
4. A concrete recommendation for THIS repo: file layout, format, how runSession loads it, how the version id is exposed (for eval reports + PostHog events later). Keep it minimal — solo founder, boring tooling, no prompt-management SaaS.

Deliver: (a) short survey of what each source actually does/recommends with links, (b) the trade-off that matters most for our three requirements, (c) one concrete recommendation (layout + format + loading + version-id exposure), (d) anything that contradicts the session.v1.md proposal.

## (a) What the sources actually do

**OpenAI — moving *away* from hosted prompt objects, toward prompts-in-repo.** This is the most directly relevant finding. OpenAI is **deprecating reusable prompt objects**: creation de-emphasized **June 3, 2026**, `v1/prompts` shuts down **Nov 30, 2026**. Their migration guide tells teams to move prompt content "into your application code" for "more control over review, testing, deployment, and versioning," specifically: create a small `prompts/` module, keep each prompt as a **named builder function**, "replace prompt variables with typed function parameters," add "lightweight eval fixtures so prompt changes are reviewed like product logic," and "move versioning to your repo using git commits, PR review, and tests or evals." They name `prompts/supportReply.ts` — **TypeScript, not markdown** — and say git history, PR review, release tags and feature flags handle versions/rollbacks "rather than API-based identifiers." ([migration guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompting/migrate-from-prompt-object), [prompting guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompting))

**PostHog — the flag payload carries a *reference*, and PostHog expects to host the content.** Payload shape is `{ "prompt_name": ..., "prompt_version": ... }` — a lightweight key, **not** the full prompt string. But their documented flow is: read payload → **fetch the matching version from PostHog** → compile → call through their AI wrapper. Prompts are hosted by them (immutable sequential versions, labels as pointers, a `config` JSON blob for model params, runtime fetch with caching/fallback). Attribution rides on `$ai_prompt_name` / `$ai_prompt_version` on `$ai_generation`, plus `$feature_flag_called` for exposure. **Not documented: tagging generations with those properties when the prompt lives in your own repo.** Also note `getFeatureFlagPayload()` is deprecated in favor of `evaluateFlags()` + `flags.getFlagPayload()`. ([LLM prompt experiments](https://posthog.com/docs/experiments/llm-prompt-experiments), [prompt management](https://posthog.com/docs/prompt-management), [node flags](https://posthog.com/docs/feature-flags/installation/nodejs))

**Langfuse / Braintrust — immutable versions + labels-as-pointers.** Langfuse: every save creates an immutable sequential version (1,2,3…); labels (`production`, `staging`) are pointers to exactly one version; rollback = repoint the label; pin in evals via `version=1` or `label="staging"`. Braintrust identifies prompts by **slug** (their own cookbook literally uses `brand-support-v1` / `brand-support-v2`) and supports `braintrust pull`/`push` to keep prompts in git for PR review. ([Langfuse version control](https://langfuse.com/docs/prompt-management/features/prompt-version-control), [Langfuse CI/CD](https://langfuse.com/resources/engineering/prompt-cicd), [Braintrust versioning](https://www.braintrust.dev/docs/cookbook/recipes/PromptVersioning))

**Anthropic — prompts as plain `.md` files, no version in filename.** The cookbook's agent patterns keep `citations_agent.md`, `research_lead_agent.md`, `research_subagent.md` in a `prompts/` dir — descriptive names, **no `v1` suffixes**, no frontmatter. ([claude-cookbooks](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-cookbooks/tree/main/patterns/agents/prompts))

**Hamel Husain (practitioner consensus) — git, and be skeptical of registries.** Storing prompts in git "treats them as software artifacts that are versioned, reviewed, and deployed atomically with the application code." His caution is pointed: "Prompt management tools are inherently limiting because they can't easily execute your application's code," risking "additional layers of indirection." ([evals FAQ](https://hamel.dev/blog/posts/evals-faq/how-should-i-version-and-manage-prompts.html))

**dotprompt — real but Genkit-gravity.** Active (~559 stars), YAML frontmatter + Handlebars, implementations across JS/Go/Python/Java/Rust. Frontmatter carries `model`, `input.schema`, `output.format` — **no version field for the prompt itself**. Adds a Handlebars dependency and a schema layer you'd otherwise get free from Zod, which you already have. ([google/dotprompt](https://github.com/google/dotprompt), [Genkit docs](https://genkit.dev/docs/js/dotprompt/))

## (b) The trade-off that matters most

Your three requirements do **not** pull equally — two are cheap and one is the real constraint:

- Eval pinning and reviewable diffs are both satisfied by **git alone**. Fixtures pin a commit; diffs are diffs.
- **Runtime loading of an arbitrary served version is the requirement that actually shapes the design.** It's the only one that forces *multiple versions to coexist in one deployed artifact*. Everything else is free.

So the decision is: **does a PostHog flag ever need to serve a version that isn't the one in the current deploy?** If no, versions are sequential-in-git and you need exactly one file. If yes, old versions must ship in the bundle, and you need a map of id → text.

The honest answer for a solo founder: **you can't run a meaningful prompt A/B test on a journaling app for a long time.** Experiments need hundreds of sessions per arm for significance. Until then, "serve a different prompt version at runtime" is speculative. And note the counter-pressure — filename versioning *destroys* the diff review you listed as requirement (c): `v1.md → v2.md` renders as whole-file add + delete, so the reviewer sees no diff at all. Git-only versioning is the only option that satisfies eval pinning and diff review *simultaneously and for free*.

## (c) Concrete recommendation

**One file, git-versioned, no version in the filename.** `apps/agent/src/session-prompt.ts` — a named builder function, exactly OpenAI's documented pattern:

```ts
// apps/agent/src/session-prompt.ts
export const PROMPT_ID = "session/2026-08-21";  // bump by hand on a real change

export const sessionPrompt = (set: QuestionSet) =>
  `You are a journaling assistant. ...
Questions:
${set.questions.map(...).join("\n")}`;
```

Then in `runSession`, return `promptId: PROMPT_ID` alongside `summary`/`answers`, so eval reports and future PostHog events both have the id without further plumbing.

**Why `.ts` and not `session.v1.md` — a verified mechanical reason, not taste.** I tested it: `tsc` **does not copy `.md` into `outDir`**. My scratch build with `src/prompts/session.md` emitted `dist/main.js` and nothing else — the markdown never shipped, and the compiled JS crashed at runtime trying to read it. Your `apps/agent` builds via `tsc --build` to `dist/`, and `apps/agent/.vercel/project.json` shows this deploys to Vercel. A `.md` prompt would work in local `node src/cli.ts` and then break in the built/deployed artifact. Making it work means a copy step in `package.json`, or `"resolveJsonModule"`-style asset handling, or a bundler plugin — all of which is new machinery to buy a format you don't need. A `.ts` export compiles, bundles and deploys with zero config, and keeps the placeholder type-safe (`set.questions` is checked; `{{questions}}` in a template is not).

You also already have `defaultQuestionSet` as a plain `.ts` export — same pattern, same rung of the ladder.

**When the flag payload actually arrives** (issue #5): keep the payload as `{model, promptId}`, and add old versions only when you genuinely run a live experiment:

```ts
const PROMPTS = { "session/2026-08-21": sessionPrompt, "session/2026-11-02": sessionPromptV2 };
```

That's a one-line change from the above, which is exactly why you shouldn't build it now.

## (d) What contradicts the `session.v1.md` proposal

1. **Filename versioning kills your own requirement (c).** `v1.md → v2.md` is an add + delete in review, not a diff. You'd be trading away diff review to buy multi-version loading you can't yet use. Note Anthropic's cookbook prompts carry **no** version suffix.
2. **`.md` doesn't survive your build — verified.** `tsc` emitted no `.md` into `dist/`; the compiled entrypoint failed to load it. Works in dev, breaks when deployed.
3. **`v1` in the name implies a registry you don't have.** Braintrust's `-v1`/`-v2` slugs work because a service resolves them; a bare filename gives you an id with no resolver and no immutability guarantee.
4. **The industry is moving the other direction.** OpenAI is actively retiring hosted prompt IDs and telling teams to use typed builder functions in a `prompts/` module with git as the version store — a `.md` artifact with a hand-rolled id is the pattern they're deprecating.
5. **Watch out — unrelated but load-bearing:** AI SDK v7 docs state the system-prompt property is **`instructions`**, and that "system messages in `prompt` or `messages` are rejected by default." `session.ts:110` passes `system:` on `ai@7.0.70`. Worth confirming against your exact pinned version before touching this file, since the prompt extraction lands right there.

**Bottom line:** skip the versioned filename and the markdown. One `session-prompt.ts` with an exported `PROMPT_ID`, git as the version store, multi-version map added the day you actually launch an experiment.</result>

name: CI

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

# Supersede in-flight runs for the same ref; ci-ok stays pending on cancellation.
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  changes:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      pull-requests: read
    outputs:
      agent: ${{ steps.filter.outputs.agent }}
      app: ${{ steps.filter.outputs.app }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: dorny/paths-filter@v4
        id: filter
        with:
          filters: |
            agent:
              - 'apps/agent/**'
              - 'packages/**'
              - 'package.json'
              - 'pnpm-lock.yaml'
              - 'pnpm-workspace.yaml'
              - 'tsconfig*.json'
              - 'biome.json'
              - '.nvmrc'
              - '.github/workflows/ci.yml'
            app:
              - 'apps/app/**'
              - '.github/workflows/ci.yml'

  agent:
    needs: changes
    if: needs.changes.outputs.agent == 'true'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v6
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: pnpm
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm lint
      - run: pnpm typecheck
      - run: pnpm -r --if-present test

  app:
    needs: changes
    if: needs.changes.outputs.app == 'true'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: apps/app
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with:
          channel: stable
          flutter-version-file: apps/app/.fvmrc
          cache: true
      - run: flutter pub get
      - run: dart format --set-exit-if-changed .
      - run: flutter analyze

  # The single required check. Green only if every job succeeded or was skipped.
  ci-ok:
    needs: [changes, agent, app]
    if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - if: contains(needs.*.result, 'failure') || contains(needs.*.result, 'cancelled')
        run: exit 1

## Why

The offline half of the two-layer eval story (ADR 0003 / README): deterministic fixtures against the live cheap model, gating CI before anything ships. Grilled + researched in session; key decisions below.

## Decisions (from the grilling)

- **No eval framework — raw \`node --test\`.** Research verified: no first-party Vercel/AI SDK evals exist (\`ai/test\` is unit mocks), promptfoo's multi-turn machinery assumes chat-shaped targets (ours terminates on a \`complete_session\` tool call), Evalite is dormant. \`runSession\` already is the harness via the \`SessionClient\` seam.
- **Split gates:** deterministic protocol eval on every agent-path PR (temperature 0, one retry); judged behavior eval nightly at 3 runs / 2-of-3 per scenario (judge: \`claude-haiku-4.5\`, one structured call per session).
- **Prompt versioning (#16): git is the registry.** \`session-prompt.ts\` exports \`sessionPrompt()\` + \`PROMPT_ID\`; no versioned filenames (kills diff review), no \`.md\` (verified: tsc doesn't ship it to dist). \`runSession\` returns \`promptId\`; also switched \`system:\` → \`instructions:\` (deprecated alias in ai v7).
- **Cost:** token-math via \`MODEL_RATES\` (the gateway response carries no cost field — verified in shipped types). Reported per run, gated at a loose 1¢ ceiling.

## Live results

- Protocol: full 10-question session **\$0.00375** (≈11¢/month for a daily poweruser, pre-caching)
- Behavior baseline (3 runs each): opening 2/3 · question-lookalike 3/3 · end-lookalike 2/3 · out-of-context 2/3 — after example-driven prompt tuning that fixed a real regression the harness caught (the model ended sessions on goodbye-lookalikes)
- Legacy fixture rubrics that are now enforced by contract schemas (single question per ask, summary as tool arg) became type assertions — not judged

## Infra

- GitHub Actions environment \`ci\` with its own gateway key (\`emotely-ci\`, \$5/month budget); eval step skips on forks
- \`nightly-evals.yml\` at 03:00 UTC + manual dispatch
- Workspace package \`license\` fields (follow-up promised in #17)

content.text:
The eval ran for real in CI — the report line is right there in the log: `cost=$0.00390` for the full live session, and the whole agent job still finished in 37s.

**[PR #18](https://github.com/trost-systems/emotely/pull/18) is up and green, ready for your review** — closing both #3 and #16. What it contains:

- **No framework — raw `node --test`**, as decided: `runSession` is the harness through the `SessionClient` seam.
- **Protocol eval (PR gate):** full live 10-question session, per-question type + `min_answers` assertions, temperature 0 + one retry, cost gated at a loose 1¢ ceiling. Live cost: **~$0.004/session** — about 11¢/month for a daily poweruser, before caching.
- **Behavior eval (nightly, 03:00 UTC + manual):** the four legacy scenarios ported as judged rubrics (one structured `claude-haiku-4.5` judge call per session), 3 runs / 2-of-3. Baseline: 2/3 · 3/3 · 2/3 · 2/3.
- **The harness already earned its keep:** it caught a real regression — the model was ending sessions on goodbye-lookalikes ("No, that's all for today") — fixed with example-driven prompt tuning, legacy-style.
- **#16 done per research:** `session-prompt.ts` + `PROMPT_ID` (`session/2026-08-21`), git as the version registry, `promptId` in every session result; also migrated `system:` → `instructions:` (deprecated in ai v7).
- Plus: `emotely-ci` gateway key (own $5 budget) as an environment secret, eval step skips on forks, and the package `license` fields promised in #17.

Two notes: the nightly workflow can only be manually dispatched once it's on `main` (GitHub requires that), so its first proof-run comes after merge. And your borderline 2/3 pass rates are exactly the baseline data issue #4's model benchmark will feed on — `glm-4.7-flash` is passable but not comfortable, which is what the benchmark exists to decide.

content.text:
All 11 review threads are addressed, replied to, and resolved, and CI is green on the fix commit (`0c8b6d4`) — including the live protocol eval in the agent job. [PR #18](https://github.com/trost-systems/emotely/pull/18) is ready for re-review.

The substantive changes, beyond the mechanical fixes:

- **"fail load" (CI eval step):** now fails loudly when the key is missing — only fork PRs (which can't have secrets) skip, with an explicit `::error::` otherwise.
- **Action pinning:** every `uses:` in both workflows is pinned to a commit SHA with a version comment; created [issue #19](https://github.com/trost-systems/emotely/issues/19) for Dependabot auto-updates of the pins (github-actions + npm ecosystems), since no existing issue covered it.
- **Judge model:** benched your suggestions live against the gateway. `deepseek-v4-flash` (both variants) and `gpt-oss-120b` **cannot hold the structured verdict schema** through the gateway (0–1 of 5 attempts); `qwen3.7-flash` holds schema but misjudges (1/5 correct); **`alibaba/qwen3.7-plus` scored 5/5 on both** and is now the default — open source, $0.40/M, and a different family than the GLM candidate it grades. No GLM-5.x exists on the gateway as of today; `glm-4.7` is still the newest zai line.
- **Prompt versioning:** `session/2026-08-21` → sequential `session/v1`, so multiple same-day changes just bump the counter.
- **Lint warnings:** all 6 non-null assertions fixed, and `noNonNullAssertion` is now an *error* — the answer to "why doesn't CI fail?" is that biome warnings don't fail `biome ci`; now this one will.
- Behavior eval also became crash-tolerant: a run where the model emits malformed tool input counts as a failed run instead of aborting the whole scenario (a real flake I hit while re-benching).

All suites re-verified after the changes: 20 unit tests, protocol eval ($0.00396 live), and all four behavior scenarios pass with the new judge.

Both in flight: the nightly fix agent (isolated worktree, will open a PR but not merge) and the gateway/caching research agent resumed with its big finding intact.

On your #4 answers — all locked, with these refinements captured:

- **Q2, latency weighted higher:** the benchmark will measure per-round latency (time from request to the model's tool call — that's the number the user feels between widgets) and rank on it first, with cost as a ceiling rather than a score. Given your margin guidance that's the right shape anyway: **any model under ~€1/month per poweruser is eligible (≈ $0.036/session; glm-4.7-flash runs at $0.004, so there's ~9× headroom), and among eligible models the fastest reliable one wins.** That opens the door to Haiku 4.5, the non-lite Gemini Flash line, GPT-5 mini etc. — I'll put them in the candidate list. This revises ADR 0003's "well under 50¢, frontier out" framing; I'll add a dated amendment to the ADR in the #4 PR rather than leave the docs contradicting the decision.
- **Q3, the reminder:** a reminder you have to act on is the thing you'll forget; I'd rather have a **monthly scheduled workflow that re-runs the benchmark itself** and opens an issue with the ranking table plus any *new* tool-capable models that appeared in the gateway catalog since the last run. Costs cents, and the issue only needs a decision, not work. Skipped: a bare calendar reminder.
- **Q5, gpt-oss-120b:** almost certainly tooling, not capability. It failed as a **judge**, not in a session: `generateObject` through the gateway falls back to tool-mode JSON, and gpt-oss's "harmony" response format (reasoning channels) through whichever provider backs it on the gateway didn't yield parseable verdict JSON — 0/5 attempts, which smells like a serving mismatch rather than a 120B model being unable to fill a 3-field schema. The session benchmark exercises a different path (plain tool calling), so I'll keep it as a candidate there and we'll see; as a judge it's not worth fighting.

I'll start the benchmark build as soon as the research lands (the gateway finding about PostHog + OTel changes how the caching/observability side is wired, so it's worth the wait). You'll get notified when the nightly-fix PR is up.

## (a) Gateway comparison — recommendation: **stay on Vercel AI Gateway**

| | **Vercel AI Gateway** | **OpenRouter** |
|---|---|---|
| **Token markup** | **0%** — "AI Gateway charges no markup and no platform fee on tokens" | **0%** — "no markup on inference pricing" |
| **Payment fees** | Credits; you pay payment-processing fees (Enterprise can invoice) | Credits: **5.5% + $0.80 min** (Stripe), 5% crypto |
| **BYOK** | **No markup or fee**; auto-retries with system creds on failure | **5%** of normal cost above monthly allowance |
| **PostHog path (ai@7)** | Works — OTel span processor | Works — same OTel span processor |
| **Model switching** | Bare `'creator/model'` string | Bare `'creator/model'` string |
| **Routing** | `order`/`only`/`sort: 'cost'\|'ttft'\|'tps'`, provider timeouts, model fallbacks | Comparable |
| **Add-on costs** | Custom Reporting $0.075/1k writes, ZDR/allowlist $0.10/1k — **all off by default** | — |

**The ADR's deciding criterion is now void.** ADR 0003 defers the choice on "OpenRouter has a *dedicated* PostHog install path; Vercel AI Gateway is listed as 'supported'." That distinction does not survive contact with ai@7:

- PostHog's OpenRouter page installs `@posthog/ai/openai` — an **OpenAI-client wrapper**, not an AI SDK path. Adopting it means abandoning `generateText`, hand-rolling the tool loop, and **manually capturing every tool call as an `$ai_span`**. That is strictly more code than you have now.
- PostHog's Vercel AI SDK page is explicit: *"This OpenTelemetry integration is the supported path for Vercel AI SDK v7. The legacy PostHog `withTracing` wrapper supports the v5 and v6 provider interfaces and **rejects v7 models**."*
- The v7 path is a `PostHogSpanProcessor` + `registerTelemetry(new OpenTelemetry(...))` in `instrumentation.ts`. It instruments **the SDK, not the provider** — so **the gateway is invisible to PostHog**. Neither gateway has an integration advantage; the "dedicated install path" is the *worse* one here.

Net: OpenRouter costs 5.5% on credits and 5% on BYOK, and its PostHog path would force a rewrite off `generateText`. Vercel AI Gateway is 0%/0% and already works. **Decide for Vercel AI Gateway and close the deferral.**

Lock-in surface is genuinely small either way: bare model strings + an `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY`. Migration = swap base URL/key. The only gateway-specific code would be `providerOptions.gateway` — which, per (d), you don't need.

## (b) Caching — automatic for every candidate, zero code

Vercel's automatic-caching doc: *"providers like OpenAI, Google, and DeepSeek cache automatically (sometimes called 'implicit caching')… For providers with implicit caching, no modification is needed and caching works automatically."* `caching: 'auto'` exists **only** to inject `cache_control` markers for Anthropic and MiniMax. Note `implicit-caching` is a per-model catalog tag, not a per-request setting — and cheap models with large static prefixes are exactly the case it pays off on. Prices $/Mtok:

| Model | In | Out | Cache read | Caching | Auto? | Ctx |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| alibaba/qwen3.7-flash | 0.030 | 0.130 | **0.006** (5×) | implicit | yes | 991k |
| openai/gpt-oss-20b | 0.050 | 0.200 | — | implicit | yes | 131k |
| zai/glm-4.7-flashx | 0.060 | 0.400 | **0.010** (6×) | implicit | yes | 200k |
| zai/glm-4.7-flash *(current)* | 0.070 | 0.400 | — | implicit | yes | 200k |
| deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash | 0.130 | 0.260 | 0.028 | implicit | yes | 1M |
| google/gemini-2.5-flash-lite | 0.100 | 0.400 | **0.010** (10×) | implicit | yes | 1M |
| openai/gpt-oss-120b | 0.100 | 0.500 | — | implicit | yes | 131k |
| **alibaba/qwen3.5-flash** | 0.100 | 0.400 | 0.001 | **none** | **no** | 1M |

Two caveats worth carrying into the benchmark: `qwen3.5-flash` has cache pricing in the catalog but **no `implicit-caching` tag** — treat it as uncached. And `glm-4.7-flash`/`gpt-oss-*` are tagged `implicit-caching` but expose **no `input_cache_read` price**, so the discount rate is unverifiable from the catalog — measure it, don't assume it.

Your loop is the ideal shape for this: 25 sequential rounds that append to a growing prefix, so each round re-reads what the last one wrote.

## (c) Cheapest tool-use candidates (live catalog, 351 models)

Beyond the table above, these are cheaper than your current pick and **belong in the #4 benchmark**:

| Model | In | Out | Cache read | Ctx | Released |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **alibaba/qwen3.7-flash** | 0.030 | 0.130 | 0.006 | 991k | 2026-07-28 |
| amazon/nova-micro | 0.035 | 0.140 | — (none) | 128k | 2024-12-03 |
| arcee-ai/trinity-mini | 0.045 | 0.150 | — (none) | 131k | 2025-12-01 |
| **nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning** | 0.050 | 0.200 | 0.010 | 262k | **2026-08-11** |
| openai/gpt-5-nano | 0.050 | 0.400 | 0.005 | 400k | 2025-08-07 |
| **inclusionai/ling-3.0-flash** | 0.060 | 0.180 | 0.012 | 256k | **2026-08-06** |
| deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-0731 | 0.076 | 0.153 | 0.014 | 1M | 2026-04-23 |
| meta/muse-spark-1.2-contributor | 0.100 | 0.200 | 0.002 | 1M | 2026-08-05 |

**Headline: `alibaba/qwen3.7-flash` is 2.3× cheaper on input and 3.1× cheaper on output than your current `zai/glm-4.7-flash`, with published cache-read pricing and 991k context.** Three of these shipped in the last three weeks — exactly why the ADR's "chosen empirically, never pinned from memory" rule is right.

Also note: newer Gemini flash-lite generations are **more expensive, not less** (3.1 = 0.25, 3.5 = 0.30 vs 2.5 = 0.10). Don't assume newer means cheaper.

## (d) Code changes for prompt caching: **none required** — but your cost math is wrong

Caching needs no code. However, `apps/agent/src/session.ts:135-136` accumulates only `inputTokens`/`outputTokens`, and `cost.ts` multiplies input by a single `inputPerM`. I confirmed from the installed `ai@7.0.70` source (`asLanguageModelUsage`) that:

```js
inputTokens: usage.inputTokens.total,
inputTokenDetails: { noCacheTokens: ..., cacheReadTokens: ..., cacheWriteTokens: ... }
```

**`inputTokens` is the total and is inclusive of cache reads.** So today the cost model bills every cached token at full rate — it will **overstate cost and hide the entire caching win**, the 3-5× the ADR is banking on. Two corrections:

- The field is **`inputTokenDetails.cacheReadTokens`**, not `usage.cachedInputTokens` or `inputTokens.cacheRead` as the task assumed — neither exists in ai@7.
- **`result.totalUsage` is `@deprecated` in ai@7.0.70; use `result.usage`.** Both lines in `session.ts` use the deprecated field.

Minimum fix: track `cacheReadTokens`, add `cacheReadPerM` to `ModelRates`, and bill `(inputTokens - cacheReadTokens)` at input rate plus `cacheReadTokens` at the cache rate. That's a few lines in `cost.ts` plus one accumulator — and it's what makes the #4 benchmark measure the thing that actually decides the model.

## (e) Contradictions with ADR 0003

1. **The deferral criterion is dead.** "OpenRouter has a *dedicated* PostHog install path" no longer favors OpenRouter — on ai@7 that path is an OpenAI-client wrapper requiring manual `$ai_span` capture, while `withTracing` *rejects v7 models*. The v7 OTel path is gateway-agnostic. Recommend closing the deferral for Vercel AI Gateway.
2. **"Both work with PostHog LLM observability" is true but for a different reason than stated** — PostHog instruments the AI SDK, not the provider, so the gateway is irrelevant to observability. Integration cleanliness cannot decide this; **fees and BYOK should** (0%/0% vs 5.5%/5%).
3. **"Prompt caching on the static context prompt"** understates it. The ~1k static system prompt is the small half; the real win is the **growing conversation prefix** across 25 rounds, which implicit caching covers automatically at 5-10× discounts.
4. **`MODEL_RATES` in `cost.ts` is already stale in shape** — no cache-read rate, so it cannot express the ADR's own 3-5× savings claim.
5. **A cheaper candidate exists now** (`qwen3.7-flash`, released after the ADR), reinforcing that the model list should be regenerated from the live catalog at benchmark time.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

## Decision: \`openai/gpt-oss-120b\` is the default model

Per the ADR 0003 amendment (in this PR): eligible = protocol 3/3, every behavior scenario ≥ 2/3, ≤ ~€1/month; ranked by **p50 per-round latency** (what the user waits between widgets), cost as tiebreak. Gateway decided: Vercel AI Gateway (fees 0%/0%; observability is gateway-agnostic on ai v7).

**Final contender run** (same code minus the guard — gpt-oss's 2/3 is the exact path the guard closes):

$FINAL

**Full 12-model run** (run 3, before the judge fix — the end-lookalike column was judge noise, see below):

$RUN3

Runners-up \`gpt-5.6-luna-fast\` / \`gpt-5-nano\` / \`gpt-5.6-luna\` are clean but ~2× the latency. \`zai/glm-4.7-flash\` (the previous default) failed protocol or behavior in every one of five runs — which is also what the nightly eval has been reporting. Haiku 4.5 / Gemini 3.7 Flash pass everything but exceed the ceiling without explicit cache markers and are 3× slower. \`qwen3.7-flash\`, \`deepseek-v4-flash\`, \`gemini-2.5-flash-lite\` (loops to the round cap), \`nemotron\`, \`gpt-5-mini\`: out.

## What the benchmark found and fixed along the way

- **Lost final answer** — models ask the last question, get the answer, and call \`complete_session\` without \`record_answer\`. The loop now refuses completion while an asked question has no recorded answer (same back-pressure as \`min_answers\`). Unit-tested.
- **Fabricated answers** — some models recorded the second question's answer without asking it; the judge saw it, the machine check couldn't. Scripted clients now track what was asked; scenario, protocol-eval and benchmark checks require asked **and** answered.
- **Judge context gap** — the judge didn't know the scenario set has two questions and graded correct runs as "ended after only two questions" (contradicting itself). It now gets the question set and runs at temperature 0. This was the whole "end-lookalike cluster" in run 3.
- **Cost math** — ai v7's \`inputTokens\` is inclusive of cache reads; we were billing cached tokens at full rate and hiding the caching win. Fixed; cache hits are now reported (gpt-oss: 94–98%).
- Crash retry, early exit for all-fail models, per-question/per-scenario diagnostics, live catalog prices.

## Monthly re-run
\`monthly-benchmark.yml\` runs the benchmark on the 1st and opens an issue with the ranking plus new tool-capable models from the catalog — the reminder that does the work.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

**[PR #22](https://github.com/trost-systems/emotely/pull/22) is up and green** — closing issue #4, ready for your review.

**The decision: `openai/gpt-oss-120b` becomes the default.** On the final code it's 3/3 protocol, perfect behavior, **p50 647 ms / p95 1.3 s** — roughly half the latency of the three clean runners-up (`gpt-5.6-luna-fast`, `gpt-5-nano`, `gpt-5.6-luna` at 1.1–1.2 s) — at ~$0.11/month with 94–98% cache hits. Your instinct about gpt-oss-120b failing as a *judge* being tooling was right; as a *session* model it's the best thing on the gateway for this task.

**What the five benchmark runs surfaced** (each fixed before deciding, all in the PR):
- **Lost final answer** — models ask the last question and call `complete_session` without recording it. The loop now refuses completion while an asked question is unrecorded. This was the whole "protocol wobble".
- **Fabricated answers** — some models recorded an answer without asking; now a deterministic violation.
- **Judge context gap** — the judge didn't know the set has two questions and failed correct runs; it now gets the set and runs at temperature 0. That explained the entire run-3 end-lookalike cluster.
- **Cost math** was billing cached tokens at full rate, hiding the caching win.

**The nightly you flagged** was red because of `glm-4.7-flash` — it failed protocol or behavior in all five runs. Merging #22 should turn the nightly green; after merge I'd also dispatch `monthly-benchmark.yml` once by hand to prove the issue-creation path.

One reviewer note to anticipate: the PR-gate eval bills gpt-oss cache reads at the input rate because the catalog publishes no cache price for it — conservative, so real cost is lower than the $0.0037 shown.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

We will wire PostHog (EU or US cloud TBD): LLM observability with privacyMode ON (journal text must NEVER reach PostHog — metadata only), feature-flag-driven model selection (payload like {model, promptId}), and native error tracking. Prior research established: for ai v7, PostHog's supported LLM-observability path is an OpenTelemetry span processor (`PostHogSpanProcessor`), and the legacy `withTracing` wrapper rejects v7 models; also `getFeatureFlagPayload()` is deprecated in favor of `evaluateFlags()` + `flags.getFlagPayload()`.

1. **Exact packages + versions to pin** (npm, today): `posthog-node`, `@posthog/ai`, any OTel packages the span-processor path needs (@opentelemetry/sdk-*?). Peer-dep constraints with ai@7.

3. **Privacy mode on the OTel path**: how to keep prompt/completion CONTENT out of `$ai_generation` events on the span-processor path (privacyMode equivalent, span attribute filtering, or config).
